reference.source: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
clinicalPearls: In younger patients tears usually follow a twisting injury on a loaded, flexed knee; in older patients they are often degenerative and may occur with minimal trauma
Typical symptoms are joint-line pain, an effusion developing over a day or so, and mechanical features such as clicking, catching, or locking
A knee locked in flexion that cannot be fully extended suggests a displaced bucket-handle tear and warrants prompt treatment
Joint-line tenderness and provocative rotation tests (e.g. McMurray's) support the diagnosis, and MRI is the investigation of choice
The peripheral (outer) third of the meniscus is vascular and can heal, favouring repair, whereas the avascular inner portion has poor healing potential
Repair is preferred where feasible, especially in younger patients with peripheral tears, to preserve meniscal function; partial meniscectomy is reserved for irreparable tears
Meniscus preservation is important because meniscectomy increases contact stress and the long-term risk of osteoarthritis
Degenerative tears in older knees with early arthritis often respond as well to conservative management and rehabilitation as to arthroscopic surgery
reference.pathophysiology: The menisci are fibrocartilaginous, wedge-shaped structures that deepen the tibial articular surface, distribute load, absorb shock, and contribute to joint stability and lubrication. A twisting force on a weight-bearing flexed knee shears the meniscus between the femoral and tibial condyles, producing longitudinal, radial, horizontal, or complex tears; a longitudinal tear whose free fragment displaces into the notch forms a bucket-handle lesion that can block extension. With age the meniscal tissue degenerates and tears more readily under low loads. Only the peripheral third has a blood supply capable of healing, so the location of a tear largely determines whether repair or excision is appropriate. Loss of meniscal tissue raises articular contact pressures and predisposes to degenerative change.
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the knee to characterise the tear and assess associated ligament and cartilage injury
Clinical joint-line palpation and provocative tests (e.g. McMurray's, Apley's grind)
Plain radiographs to assess for degenerative change or loose bodies and to exclude fracture
Diagnostic arthroscopy in selected cases where imaging is equivocal and intervention is planned
redFlags: A truly locked knee unable to fully extend, suggesting a displaced bucket-handle tear needing prompt surgery
Acute tense haemarthrosis suggesting a significant associated injury such as an ACL rupture
Hot, swollen, systemically unwell knee raising concern for septic arthritis
Signs of associated ligamentous instability or fracture
reference.prognosis: Peripheral tears repaired successfully can restore durable meniscal function, while small stable tears may settle with conservative care; extensive meniscectomy relieves mechanical symptoms but increases the long-term likelihood of osteoarthritis, and degenerative tears in already arthritic knees have a more limited response to surgery.
pitfalls: Performing meniscectomy on a degenerative tear in an arthritic knee that would do as well with rehabilitation
Removing repairable peripheral tissue rather than attempting repair, accelerating arthritis
Missing a locked knee from a displaced bucket-handle tear
Overlooking a concurrent ACL injury that leaves the meniscal repair at risk of re-tear
references: Apley & Solomon's System of Orthopaedics and Fractures
